questions.question: Select the word segment that can substitute the bracketed word segment correctly and complete the sentence meaningfully. The detective solved the mystery (very clever with the few clues) he found.
questions.questionHtml:
Select the word segment that can substitute the bracketed word segment correctly and complete the sentence meaningfully.

The detective solved the mystery (very clever with the few clues) he found.

options.text: very cleverly with the few clues
options.html: very cleverly with the few clues

options.text: much clever with the few clues
options.html: much clever with the few clues

options.text: very cleverly with the few clue
options.html: very cleverly with the few clue

questions.solution:
The error in the bracketed segment "very clever with the few clues" is the use of the adjective "clever" to modify the verb "solved." An adverb is needed to describe how the detective solved the mystery.

a) "very cleverly with the few clues" - This option correctly uses the adverb "cleverly" to modify the verb "solved." "Very" is an intensifier for the adverb.

b) "much clever with the few clues" - "Clever" is an adjective and cannot modify the verb "solved." "Much" can intensify comparatives or certain verbs, but not a simple adjective in this way to modify another verb.

c) "very cleverly with the few clue" - "few clue" is grammatically incorrect as "clue" should be plural "clues" when modified by "few".

d) "more cleverly with few clue" - "More cleverly" would be a comparative adverb. While "cleverly" is correct, "few clue" is grammatically incorrect as "clue" should be plural "clues" when modified by "few," and typically "the few clues" (as in the original sentence) if referring to specific ones.

The correct sentence is: The detective solved the mystery very cleverly with the few clues he found.

Hence, the most appropriate choice is option a).

questions.solution:
The subject of the Passive Voice is changed into the object of the Active Voice. Also, the object of the Passive Voice is changed into the subject of the Active Voice.

The removal of the "to be" verb ['being' here] and the preposition 'by' is necessary while changing the voice of the sentence from Passive to Active.

The Passive voice in this question is in Past Continuous tense. Thus, the Active voice will also be in Past Continuous.

In Passive voice, the format is: Object of the Active voice (Subjective case) + was/were + being + V3 + by + Subject of the Active voice (Objective case).

Thus, the format of Active voice is: Subject + was/were + V1 + ing + Object.

For example:

A document was being typed by Arnab. (Passive Voice)

Arnab was typing a document. (Active Voice)

The options except (b) don't follow the correct grammatical format of the Active Voice.

Hence, the correct answer is option (b).

Note:

V1 -> Base form/simple form of verb, V2 -> Past form of verb (-ed form or irregular verb), V3 -> Past participle form of verb (-ed, -d, -t, -en, or -n), V4 -> Continuous form of verb / Present participle form of verb (-ing form), V5 -> Third person singular (V1+ -es or -s).

A Preposition is a word placed before a noun or a pronoun or a noun equivalent (pronoun, adverb, gerund, infinitive, adverbial clause, or any clause that can be used as the object of the preposition) and shows a relationship in space or time or a logical relationship between two or more people, places, or things in a sentence.

Examples

I. The teacher scolded the child for being late.

II. We're going to a party.

· The words in bold are called prepositions because they normally take position before (pre) a noun/pronoun or a noun equivalent (pronoun, adverb, gerund, infinitive, adverbial clause, or any clause that can be used as the object of the preposition.

· The noun/pronoun which is used with a preposition is called its Object.

questions.solution:
The sentence in the Indirect Speech is in Simple Past Tense. Therefore, the sentence in the Direct Speech will be in Simple Present Tense.

Simple Past (Subject +V2 + Object) will be converted into Simple Present (Subject +V1st + Object).

For example:

He said that he never went to the village. (Indirect Speech)

He said, "I never go to the village." (Direct Speech)

The following things in the sentence will change when changed from Indirect Speech to Direct Speech:

· 'That' is removed and inverted commas ("...") is placed.

· The pronoun 'she' is changed into 'I' and 'that morning' is changed into 'this morning'.

· The verbs 'wondered' and 'had' (simple past tense) are changed into 'wonder' and 'has' (simple present tense) respectively.

Option (a) is eliminated because the verb 'wondered' is Simple Past tense. Option (b) is eliminated because the verb 'have wondered' is Present Perfect tense. Option (c) is eliminated because 'the old' is used.

Option (d) is the correct answer.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Jennie said, "I wonder what that old trouble-maker has on his mind this morning."

• Afforestation

○ Afforestation is the process of planting trees in areas with little or no tree cover, such as abandoned farmland, deserts, or industrial sites.

○ Unlike reforestation, which involves planting trees in shrinking forests, afforestation focuses on new areas.

• Benefits of Afforestation:

○ Soil Conservation: Prevents soil erosion and helps maintain soil fertility.

○ Reduction of Carbon Dioxide: Lowers carbon dioxide levels in the atmosphere.

○ Flood Control: Helps manage floods by improving water filtration and reducing flood size.

○ Crop Production: Enhances crop yields and protects crops from wind and sunlight.

○ Sustainability: Makes semiarid lands more sustainable for future use.

• Article 329 of the Constitution of India bars the interference of the courts in electoral matters

• Article 324 called for the Superintendence, direction and control of the elections to be vested in the Election commission of India.

• Article 326 of the Indian Constitution states that the elections of the House of the People and the Legislative Assemblies of the States are based on adult suffrage.

• Article 327 talks about the Power of the Parliament to make provision with respect to the elections to the legislature.

Further Insight:

• Articles Related to Elections and the Election Commission

○ Article 324:

■ Establishes the Election Commission of India (ECI) to oversee and ensure free and fair elections in the country. It grants the President the authority to appoint the Chief Election Commissioner and other Election Commissioners.

○ Article 325:

■ Provides for the creation of a common electoral roll for elections to the Lok Sabha and State Legislative Assemblies, ensuring that all citizens who are eligible can vote.

○ Article 326:

■ States that elections to the Lok Sabha and State Legislative Assemblies will be based on adult suffrage, meaning all citizens above the age of 18 are eligible to vote.

○ Article 327:

■ Empowers Parliament to make provisions for the conduct of elections to the Lok Sabha and to the State Legislatures.

○ Article 328:

■ Allows the State Legislatures to make provisions for the conduct of elections to the Legislative Assemblies of the states and to the offices of Chairpersons of Panchayats at different levels.

○ Article 329:

■ Prohibits the interference of courts in electoral matters, ensuring that the validity of elections is not questioned in a court of law.

○ Article 330:

■ Provides for the reservation of seats for Scheduled Castes (SCs) and Scheduled Tribes (STs) in the Lok Sabha and State Legislative Assemblies.

○ Article 331:

■ Empowers the President to nominate representatives of the Anglo-Indian community to the Lok Sabha if he/she believes that the community is not adequately represented.

○ Article 332:

■ Allows the reservation of seats for SCs and STs in the Legislative Assemblies of the states.

○ Article 333:

■ Empowers the Governor of a state to nominate not more than two members of the Anglo-Indian community to the Legislative Assembly if he/she feels that the community is not adequately represented.

○ Article 334:

■ Relates to the reservation of seats for SCs and STs, and the Anglo-Indian community, and provides for their continuation for a period of ten years from the commencement of the Constitution, which has been extended multiple times.

Indian black cotton soils (regur) are predominantly "Vertisols" - clay-rich soils (montmorillonitic) with high CEC, deep cracks in dry season, and strong shrink - swell behavior. They are agriculturally significant for cotton, sorghum, and pulses.

- "A": "Alfisols" are moderately leached soils with subsurface clay accumulation, often under deciduous forests.

- "C": "Oxisols" are highly weathered, iron - aluminum oxide-rich tropical soils with low CEC.

- "D": "Ultisols" are acidic, strongly leached soils with low base saturation.

Further Insights:

- Vertisols have high water-holding capacity but poor drainage and are prone to waterlogging.

- These soils are rich in Ca and Mg carbonates but often deficient in nitrogen and available phosphorus.

- Key regions: Deccan Plateau states - Maharashtra, Madhya Pradesh, Gujarat, parts of Andhra Pradesh and Karnataka.

- Proper tilth management and contour bunding are critical for Vertisol agriculture.
